summary: SDK L2-normalize toggle causes asymmetric embedding normalization, rerank score instability, and increased queue latency
description:
Issue summary: Customer reports intermittent rerank ordering shifts and elevated queue latency after upgrading to SDK v0.9.3. Symptoms appear during high-concurrency streaming rerank jobs and correlate with the SDK's new l2-normalize toggle.

Impact: AtlasSearch observed larger-than-usual tail latencies on /v1/rerank calls (p95 -> 2.1s, p99 -> 6.8s), higher CPU fallback rates on rerank workers, and quality regressions (frequent top-k reorderings for identical queries). Production traffic affected for a subset of customers in us-east over the last 48 hours.

Environment: Production, us-east, Dedicated rerank pool for AtlasSearch (customer enterprise tier). SDK version reported by customer: 0.9.3; server runtime: serving-runtime 2.7.1.

Observed behavior and logs: Support logs show bursts of 429/503-like backlog from rerank-service instrumentation when embedding batches include mixed-dimension vectors or when client-supplied embeddings include the normalization flag in metadata. Samples of similarity outputs show many similarities collapsing to near-zero for otherwise high-score pairs.

Initial investigation notes: Engineering reproduced a reduced repro locally by running a streaming rerank load with mixed embedding inputs and SDK v0.9.3. We observed that the SDK attaches an "X-Embed-Normalize: true" header when the new toggle is enabled. The serving-runtime also performs normalization by default unless feature-flagged. When both client and server normalize, numerical underflow and unexpected float reductions occur for certain quantized representations, particularly when mixing 1536-dim and 1024-dim embeddings in the same batch. This triggers metric shifts, cache misses for prefix/KV cache, and causes more rerank work to fall back to CPU paths, increasing queue times.

Hypothesis: Double-normalization between SDK and serving-runtime (client-side and server-side) produces asymmetric scaling and effective dimensional drift for some vectors. This makes cosine/L2 comparisons unreliable, which increases scattering in score distribution and forces extra compute and cache churn. The behavior is amplified when embedding dimensions differ within the same request batch.

Workaround: Ask customers to pin SDK to v0.9.2 or explicitly set the SDK option l2_normalize=false for v0.9.3 until server-side behavior is patched. On server side, a temporary feature-flag disable of server-side normalization for affected pools reduces the incidence of the issue. Both mitigations reduce tail latency and stabilize rerank ordering in our tests.

Resolution plan: Patch candidates in progress: 1) SDK PR to avoid sending normalization header unless user requests normalization; 2) Serving-runtime change to honor explicit header and perform idempotent normalization checks (and reject mixed-dim batches with a 400 or route to a safe path). Related PRs linked above. Aim to land hotfixes and deploy to canary pools by 2026-03-15.

Next steps: Roll hotfix to canary rerank pool in us-east, run AtlasSearch repro suite, add unit and integration tests for normalization header interplay, add server-side assertion to log and reject mixed-dim batches, and update SDK docs and release notes about the toggle. Follow up with customer once canary metrics look stable.

Notes: This ticket is customer-impacting and tied to a larger normalization compatibility workstream. Consider adding a persistent schema header (e.g., Embed-Schema: dims=1536;norm=none|l2) to reduce future ambiguity.
steps_to_reproduce:
1) Install SDK v0.9.3 with default settings.
2) Prepare a streaming rerank job that sends mixed-dimension embeddings (some 1536-dim from model A, some 1024-dim from model B) in a single batch.
3) Enable high concurrency (50+ concurrent streams) against the customer's dedicated rerank pool.
4) Observe rerank p95/p99 latency increases and score instability in top-k results, and check rerank-service logs for 'double-normalize' warnings and CPU fallback counters.
